findings.title: Hardcoded authentication bypass / backdoor credential
findings.description: 1 hardcoded credential comparison(s) or debug-gated auth bypass marker(s) found. Anyone who decompiles the APK can read these credentials and authenticate without authorization.
findings.remediation: Remove all hardcoded credentials and debug bypasses from the client. Authentication must always be verified server-side against credentials the client never stores. Gate any test login helpers behind build flavors that never ship to production, and add CI checks that fail the release build if bypass markers are present.
findings.severity_rationale: Hardcoded credentials are directly extractable from the APK and grant authentication as another user: full account compromise with trivial effort (Critical).
findings.confidence_rationale: The literal credential comparison is present verbatim in the decompiled source at the cited line; no inference required.

findings.title: Hardcoded encryption key
findings.description: Hardcoded encryption key material in 1 location(s).
findings.remediation: Do not embed keys. Generate keys at runtime with KeyGenerator and a SecureRandom, or store them in the Android Keystore (AndroidKeyStore) so key material never enters app memory as a literal. For data that must be decryptable off-device, fetch keys from a server over TLS after authentication.
findings.severity_rationale: A hardcoded key is recoverable by decompiling the APK, so every ciphertext produced with it is effectively plaintext to an attacker: total loss of confidentiality.
findings.confidence_rationale: The SecretKeySpec constructor receives a string literal, a literal byte array, or a variable provably assigned a literal in the preceding lines.

findings.title: Hardcoded test accounts in authentication code
findings.description: 2 hardcoded test-account literal(s) found in authentication code. Test accounts shipped in production builds act as standing backdoors.
findings.remediation: Remove test accounts from production builds. Provision test users in a staging backend instead, and add a release-gate check that fails the build when known test-account literals appear in auth code.

provenance.title: Hardcoded test accounts in authentication code

findings.severity_rationale: Test credentials are extractable from the APK and frequently carry elevated or shared access; compromise is realistic (High).
findings.confidence_rationale: The test-account literal appears verbatim at the cited line inside authentication-related code.

findings.title: Password hashed without a salt
findings.description: Password hashed without a salt in 1 location(s).
findings.remediation: Never store passwords as plain digests. Use Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt with a unique random salt per password via a vetted library.
findings.severity_rationale: Unsalted fast hashes let attackers use rainbow tables and GPU brute force to recover passwords, compromising user accounts.
findings.confidence_rationale: A digest() call on a password-like value with a weak MessageDigest and no salt keyword within 8 lines; the salt could theoretically be mixed in farther away.

findings.title: Cryptographic key material stored in SharedPreferences
findings.description: Possible key material in SharedPreferences in 3 location(s).
findings.remediation: Store keys in the Android Keystore (AndroidKeyStore) or use EncryptedSharedPreferences from androidx.security for sensitive values; never persist raw key material in plaintext XML.

provenance.title: Cryptographic key material stored in SharedPreferences

findings.severity_rationale: Key material in plaintext preferences XML is exposed on rooted devices and via backups, defeating the encryption it is meant to support.
findings.confidence_rationale: The preference name matches key/secret/token/password-like patterns, but the stored value was not proven to be key material statically.

findings.title: Application is debuggable
findings.snippet: application tag parsed with debuggable=true
findings.description: Application tag sets android:debuggable="true". The app can be attached by a debugger on any device with adb access.
findings.remediation: Remove android:debuggable="true" from the release manifest (or set it to false). Keep debuggable builds internal only; verify the shipped APK with `aapt dump badging` / apkanalyzer and in CI.
findings.severity_rationale: HIGH: a debuggable release build exposes the running process to debugger attachment on user devices, enabling memory inspection, secret extraction, and bypass of local protections.
findings.confidence_rationale: HIGH: the flag is a literal boolean on the application tag, parsed directly from the decoded manifest.

findings.title: Cleartext HTTP traffic explicitly allowed
findings.snippet: android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"
findings.description: android:usesCleartextTraffic="true": the app explicitly permits cleartext HTTP traffic, so sensitive data may traverse the network unencrypted.
findings.remediation: Remove android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" (or set it to false) and migrate endpoints to HTTPS. If a specific legacy host must stay on HTTP, scope the exception to that host in a network security config instead of allowing cleartext globally.
findings.severity_rationale: HIGH: cleartext HTTP exposes credentials, tokens, and PII to any passive network observer; the opt-out is global to the app.
findings.confidence_rationale: HIGH: the attribute value is read directly from the decoded manifest application tag.

findings.title: usesCleartextTraffic enabled in application manifest
findings.description: Application permits cleartext (HTTP) traffic globally.
findings.remediation: Remove android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" from the manifest (the default is false) and serve all traffic over HTTPS. If specific legacy hosts still require HTTP, use a network security configuration with narrowly scoped domain-config exceptions instead of a global flag.
findings.severity_rationale: A global cleartext opt-in disables Android's default plaintext protection for every network request, enabling passive eavesdropping and active tampering.

findings.title: Hostname verification disabled
findings.description: 1 hostname-verification bypass(es) found.
findings.remediation: Use the strict default hostname verifier (HttpsURLConnection.getDefaultHostnameVerifier()). If you must customize, compare against an allow-list of expected hostnames instead of returning true.

findings.confidence_rationale: Literal ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER tokens or source-verified verify() bodies that only return true.

findings.title: Custom SSLSocketFactory that skips certificate verification

findings.remediation: Remove the custom factory and use the platform default SSLContext. If customization is required, delegate verification to the default TrustManager or implement proper pinning.

provenance.title: Custom SSLSocketFactory that skips certificate verification

findings.confidence_rationale: Trust-all indicators co-located with SSLContext/socket-factory setup; manual review should confirm the factory is installed on real connections.

findings.title: WebView JavaScript enabled
findings.description: JavaScript enabled in a WebView that also exposes an addJavascriptInterface bridge (1 call site(s)). Web content can invoke native Java methods.
findings.remediation: Disable JavaScript unless the WebView genuinely needs it. If it is required, only load trusted HTTPS content, validate every URL in shouldOverrideUrlLoading, and never combine JavaScript with an addJavascriptInterface bridge that reaches native functionality.
findings.severity_rationale: HIGH: JavaScript plus a JS bridge lets loaded web content call into native code; this is the classic WebView bridge-escape configuration. Escalated from MEDIUM because the bridge is present.

findings.title: Token used without expiry or refresh handling
findings.description: 2 file(s) read auth/session tokens with no expiry, refresh, or deadline handling visible in the same file. Static analysis cannot confirm whether the server enforces token expiry or rotates refresh tokens; review the token lifecycle server-side before treating this as a vulnerability.
findings.remediation: Issue short-lived access tokens with explicit expiry, validate exp on every use, and implement refresh-token rotation. Enforce expiry server-side; client-side checks are defense in depth, not the control.

findings.severity_rationale: Non-expiring tokens extend the replay window after theft (Medium), but only if the server also fails to enforce expiry, which is unverified.

findings.title: AES/CBC used without observed integrity protection

findings.remediation: Prefer Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding"). If CBC must stay, add encrypt-then-MAC with HmacSHA256 over (IV || ciphertext) using an independent key, and verify the MAC before decrypting.

findings.title: Application backup enabled
findings.snippet: android:allowBackup attribute absent; Android defaults it to true
findings.description: android:allowBackup is true (defaulted (attribute absent)). App-private data can be extracted via adb backup / Auto Backup and restored elsewhere.
findings.remediation: Set android:allowBackup="false" unless backup is a genuine product requirement. If backup is required, use a restrictive android:fullBackupContent / android:dataExtractionRules file that excludes sensitive files, and encrypt sensitive data at rest.
findings.severity_rationale: MEDIUM: backup exposes app-private storage to anyone with adb access; impact depends on what sensitive data the app stores, which cannot be fully determined from the manifest alone.
findings.confidence_rationale: HIGH: allowBackup is a manifest-level boolean; when the attribute is absent Android defaults it to true, which is documented platform behavior.

findings.title: Outdated SDK policy (targetSdk / minSdk)
findings.snippet:
android:targetSdkVersion="28"

android:minSdkVersion="21"
findings.description: Weak SDK policy: targetSdkVersion=28 is below the recommended minimum of 30; minSdkVersion=21 predates the runtime-permission model (API 23): dangerous permissions are granted at install time.
findings.remediation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 30 or higher (ideally the latest) and test against the new behavior changes. Raise minSdkVersion to 23+ so the runtime permission model applies on all supported devices.
findings.severity_rationale: MEDIUM: an outdated targetSdk forfeits platform hardening applied per API level; minSdk < 23 additionally removes runtime permission control on old devices. Both widen the attack surface but do not directly disclose data by themselves.
findings.confidence_rationale: HIGH: SDK versions are literal integers from the manifest's <uses-sdk> declaration.

findings.description: 6 dangerous permission(s) across 5 sensitive group(s): Camera: CAMERA; Contacts: READ_CONTACTS; Location: ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION; Microphone: RECORD_AUDIO; SMS: READ_SMS, SEND_SMS.
findings.remediation: Request only permissions the app genuinely needs; prefer scoped alternatives (photo picker, approximate location, one-time permissions). Justify each dangerous permission in the Play Data safety section and handle denial gracefully.
findings.severity_rationale: MEDIUM: SMS, call-log, and precise/background location permissions are MEDIUM because they enable surveillance-grade data collection; other dangerous groups (contacts, camera, microphone, storage, phone, calendar, sensors) are LOW as privacy-relevant but less directly exfiltrative on their own.
findings.confidence_rationale: HIGH: permissions are literal <uses-permission> entries parsed from the manifest; Android's dangerous classification is documented platform behavior.

findings.title: Excessive permission scope

permissions: android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION

findings.description: App requests dangerous permissions from 5 distinct sensitive groups (Camera, Contacts, Location, Microphone, SMS): excessive scope for a typical app.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege: drop permission groups not required for core features, request permissions in context (when the feature is used), and re-audit third-party SDKs that may be pulling in permissions via manifest merging.
findings.severity_rationale: MEDIUM: spanning 3+ sensitive groups materially increases the privacy blast radius of compromise or SDK abuse, though scope alone does not prove data is exfiltrated.

findings.title: No network security configuration referenced
findings.snippet: android:networkSecurityConfig not declared
findings.description: No android:networkSecurityConfig is referenced in the manifest. Informational: no pinning, per-domain TLS policy, or cleartext exceptions are declared.
findings.remediation: No action required by this finding alone. Consider adding a network security config to declare certificate pinning, restrict cleartext traffic per-domain, and distrust user CAs in release builds.
findings.severity_rationale: INFORMATIONAL: the absence of a network security config is inventory metadata, not a vulnerability; it only means no declarative network controls exist.
findings.confidence_rationale: HIGH: the attribute is either present on the application tag or it is not; absence is directly observed.

findings.title: Certificate pinning presence check
findings.description: No certificate pinning detected; assess threat model. Absence alone is not a vulnerability.
findings.remediation: If your threat model includes hostile networks, add certificate pinning (e.g. OkHttp CertificatePinner or <pin-set> in the network security config) with a backup pin and a rotation plan.
findings.severity_rationale: Informational: pinning is a defense-in-depth choice, not a vulnerability by itself.
findings.confidence_rationale: Heuristic keyword search; custom or native pinning may be missed, hence medium confidence.

findings.title: Backend endpoint inventory (https hosts)
findings.description: Backend inventory: 1 distinct https host(s): api.testapp.blindspot.example
findings.remediation: Review the inventory: confirm each host is in scope, served over TLS 1.2+, and covered by the app's certificate validation.
findings.severity_rationale: Informational: inventory for scoping, not a vulnerability.
findings.confidence_rationale: Hosts taken literally from https:// strings in source.

findings.title: INTERNET permission without a network security configuration
findings.description: App uses INTERNET but declares no network security configuration.
findings.remediation: Add an explicit network security configuration declaring cleartextTrafficPermitted="false", appropriate trust anchors, and pinning where the threat model warrants it.

provenance.title: INTERNET permission without a network security configuration

findings.severity_rationale: Informational: absence of a config is not itself a vulnerability; it limits declarative transport-policy review.
findings.confidence_rationale: Manifest declares INTERNET and has no android:networkSecurityConfig attribute.

findings.title: Native library inventory
findings.description: APK ships 1 native librar(ies): lib/armeabi-v7a/libnative.so
findings.remediation: No action required from this inventory alone. Review the listed libraries for known-vulnerable versions and confirm they are built with modern hardening (PIE, RELRO, stack canaries).
findings.severity_rationale: Informational: inventory only, not a vulnerability.
findings.confidence_rationale: High: the list comes directly from the APK's lib/ entries.
